note if they are clear despite the presence of cardiac silhouette enlargement.", "Correlate the anatomical finding (widened left superior mediastinum) with the physiological symptom (hypoxaemia) by considering a Persistent Left Superior Vena Cava (PLSVC) draining into the left atrium.", "Distinguish this from left heart failure (which would typically show pulmonary venous congestion) or compressive masses (which would not inherently cause shunting/hypoxaemia without airway compromise)."]}, {"category": "diagnosis", "trigger": "When evaluating a chest X-ray with diffuse bilateral opacities to distinguish between Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) and Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema.", "steps": ["Assess the distribution and density of lung opacities: Look for persistent, diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates that may appear as a 'whiteout' or extensive consolidation, often sparing the extreme periphery or showing air bronchograms.", "Evaluate cardiac silhouette and vascular markings: Check for cardiomegaly (enlarged heart), prominent upper lobe vessels, Kerley B lines, or pleural effusions which are hallmarks of fluid overload/heart failure.", "Distinguish based on morphology: If the infiltrates are diffuse and persistent without significant cardiomegaly or specific signs of hydrostatic pressure (like cephalization), favor ARDS; if the heart is enlarged and there are signs of vascular congestion, favor cardiogenic edema."]}, {"category": "diagnosis", "trigger": "When evaluating a chest X-ray showing a focal tubular or branching opacity in the upper lobes surrounded by an area of hyperlucency.", "steps": ["Identify the primary opacity: Look for a distinct, finger-in-glove or tubular branching density representing an impacted bronchus (mucocele).", "Assess the surrounding parenchyma: Check for adjacent hyperinflation or hyperlucency caused by collateral air drift (air entering via pores of Kohn but unable to exit due to atresia).", "Distinguish from mimics: Differentiate from allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), which typically presents with bilateral, migratory, or central bronchiectasis and systemic symptoms, whereas this finding is often solitary, stable, and located in the left upper lobe.", "Differentiate from sequestration: Note that pulmonary sequestration usually presents as a solid mass (often lower lobe) with a systemic feeding vessel, rather than a tubular mucocele with surrounding hyperinflation."]}]

An 18-year-old male with a history of chronic sinusitis and recurrent lower respiratory tract infections undergoes a chest X-ray. On physical examination, heart sounds are heard best on the right side of the chest. Based on the chest X-ray in Figure 1, which of the following findings support a diagnosis of Kartagener syndrome in this patient?
A. Left-sided heart apex and right-sided horizontal fissure
B. Right-sided heart apex and left-sided horizontal fissure
C. Left-sided heart apex and left-sided horizontal fissure
D. Right-sided heart apex and right-sided horizontal fissure
E. Absence of cystic changes in the lower lobes
F. Presence of cystic changes in the upper lobes
